catalog_citation: Bradshaw, Robert L. 2007. Fuyug Grammar Sketch. Data Papers on Papua New Guinea Languages, Volume 53. Ukarumpa: SIL-PNG Academic Publications. ISBN 9980-0-3353-3.
catalog_locator: Bradshaw 2007, section 2.5 'Stress', printed p.24 (p.36); 2.4.5 'Five syllables' same page; example word lists 2.4.2-2.4.4, printed pp.22-23 (pp.34-35)…
catalog_quote: 2.4.5 Five syllables. Five syllables are found in borrowed words only, such as shown in the following list. V.CV.CV.CV.CV egelegele [ɛ'gɛlɛgɛlɛⁱ] 'well'; CV.CV.CV.CV.CV takurukuru [tɑ'kulukulu] 'white skin'. 2.5 Stress. Stress in Fuyug is predictable. It occurs on the ultimate syllable in two-syllable words (before affixation) and on the antepenultimate in three- and four-syllable words (again, before affixation). Therefore, it need not be written. Affixation does not move stress, as noted in the fourth example. 'S ge ['gɛⁱ] 'go/went'; 'SS gege 'going'; S'S alim 'yesterday'; 'SSSS hindel+ele 'coming out'; 'SSS sungulum 'fly'; S'SSS elevala 'place name'.

Affixation does not move when stress.' followed by the four examples ’S [’g-ei] /ge/ ‘go-SEP’, S’S [a’lím] /alim/ ‘yesterday’, ’SSS [’súηgulúm] /sungulum/ ‘fly’, S’SSS [e’levala] /elevala/ ‘place name’ — verbatim, including the garbled 'does not move when stress' (sic in source). Section 4.5.2 (line 580, p. 13): 'Morpheme constructions do not alter syllable patt…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog stress on syllable 2 of 2, 1 of 3, 2 of 4 (final in 2-syllable words, initial in 3-syllable, second in 4-syllable) is exactly Bradshaw's statement (final in disyllables, antepenult in 3- and 4-syllable words); the four examples on p. 9 match syllable by syllable. Bradshaw adds that the count is over the unaffixed root and that affixes do not shift stress, and that loans keep source-language stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable and depends on syllable count of the unaffixed word: final syllable in disyllables, antepenultimate in three- and four-syllable words (i.e. initial in trisyllables, second in four-syllable words); monosyllables are stressed. Affixation does not move the stress from where it falls on the root.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed. The acute accents in forms like [’súηgulúm] and [’án] mark vowel nasalization before nasal consonants (rule 5, p. 8: V --> [+nasal] / __ C[+nasal]), not secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 13, sec. 4.5.2: 'Morpheme constructions do not alter syllable patterns (nor stress placement as noted in 3.1 Stress above).' with examples [i’da] /ida/ ‘cut’ > [i’da+di] ‘cut-IRR’. Sec. 6 Loan words: 'Borrowed words follow the original language stress pattern.'
new_statements.identity_note: Bradshaw 1996 (p. 1) says its data are from the Goilala District, mainly Woitape Sub-District, 1988-1995, and that it describes the North/South Udab dialect, differing from his 1991 Organised Phonology Data and 1992 Grammar Essentials, which were based on the Central Udab dialect. The unopened SIL 42325 'Fuyuge Organised Phonology Data' is plausibly that 1991 Central-Udab OPD (or its 1996 revision), so it may describe a different dialect from the 1996 Essentials; unverified.

audit.reasoning: The deciding quotation is verbatim at the cited page of the held 2007 SIL reference grammar, which is the fullest and latest phonological description of Fuyug; Glottolog lists nothing better (only Ray 1912, read here and silent on lexical stress), the author's 1996 Phonology Essentials ms (downloaded) gives the identical ultimate-in-disyllables / antepenult-in-3-4-syllables rule plus 'borrowed words follow the original language stress pattern', and his 2021 dictionary defers to the 2007 sketch. stress on syllable 2 of 2, 1 of 3, 2 of 4 with stress computed before affixation matches the source. Only residual note: a few of Bradshaw's own list transcriptions (ale, ganing initial; endanti, kagavan penult) do not follow his rule, which could be recorded as a caution but does not warrant a reclassify.

sources.citation: Ray, Sidney H. (ed./transl., from the ms of Rev. Father Egidi). 1912. A Grammar of the Fuyuge Language. Appendix I in R. W. Williamson, The Mafulu: Mountain People of British New Guinea, pp.307-331. London: Macmillan. (Project Gutenberg #17910 text.)
sources.quote: No general word-stress rule. Only accent remarks: interrogative nouns - 'If already ending in a, the a takes a strong accent'; interrogative future formed 'with a stress upon the final a in the first conjugation'. Also notes pervasive elision of final open syllables (usually -e) phrase-internally.
sources.locator: Appendix I, 'Phonology' I-II and 'IV. Interrogative Nouns' (Gutenberg the text)
